key_terms.meaning: One experiment with exactly two outcomes, success (probability p) and failure (probability q = 1 − p).
X = number of successes in n independent Bernoulli trials with the same p; P(X = x) = C(n, x) pˣ qⁿ⁻ˣ for x = 0, 1, …, n.
Mean = np, variance = npq, standard deviation = √(npq).
X = number of rare events in a fixed interval; P(X = x) = e^(−λ) λˣ ÷ x! for x = 0, 1, 2, …
Average number of events per interval; mean = λ and variance = λ, so the standard deviation is √λ.
When n is large and p is small, take λ = np; the binomial probabilities then match the Poisson closely.
X = trial number of the first success; P(X = x) = qˣ⁻¹ p for x = 1, 2, …; mean = 1/p, variance = q/p².
X = trial number on which the r-th success occurs; P(X = x) = C(x−1, r−1) pʳ qˣ⁻ʳ for x = r, r+1, …; mean = r/p.
f(x) = 1 ÷ (b − a) on a ≤ x ≤ b and 0 outside; mean = (a + b)/2, variance = (b − a)²/12.
f(x) = λ e^(−λx) for x ≥ 0; mean = 1/λ, variance = 1/λ²; models the wait to the next Poisson event.
P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t): the past wait gives no information about the extra wait.
f(x) = 1 ÷ (σ√(2π)) × e^(−(x−μ)² ÷ 2σ²); mean μ, variance σ², symmetric bell shape.
Z = (X − μ)/σ turns any normal X into N(0, 1), whose probabilities are read from the standard normal table.
For a normal curve about 68% of values lie within μ ± σ, about 95% within μ ± 2σ, about 99.7% within μ ± 3σ.
f(x) = xᵅ⁻¹ e^(−x/θ) ÷ (Γ(α) θᵅ) for x > 0; shape α, scale θ; mean = αθ, variance = αθ².
f(x) = (k/λ)(x/λ)ᵏ⁻¹ e^(−(x/λ)ᵏ) for x > 0; shape k, scale λ; used for lifetimes and hazard rates.
X is log-normal when ln X is normal; used for products of many small positive effects; right-skewed.
The chance of failing in the next instant given survival so far; constant for exponential, increasing for Weibull with k > 1.

takeaways: Counts of yes/no outcomes in n independent trials of the same chance follow the binomial distribution, fixed by n and p alone.
Rare events in a fixed interval follow the Poisson distribution, which has one parameter λ and variance equal to its mean.
The geometric and negative binomial distributions count trials until successes, not successes in a fixed number of trials.
The uniform distribution is flat: equal density everywhere on its interval, so probability equals length of subinterval divided by total length.
The exponential distribution is the only continuous waiting-time law that is memoryless, and it comes directly from a constant-rate Poisson process.
The normal curve is fixed by μ and σ, and every normal probability is a standard normal probability after the z-transform.
Squaring and summing exponentials gives gamma; stretching a lifetime law gives Weibull; exponentiating a normal gives log-normal.
Choose a distribution from how the data are generated — counts, waits, or positive skewed measurements — not from which formula looks easy.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are scored on stating the assumptions clearly, deriving the mean and variance, and finishing with a correct numerical probability worked from the standard tables.

bank.q: State the assumptions of the binomial distribution. Derive its mean and variance, and explain what happens to the shape as p moves away from 0.5.
outline: Four assumptions: fixed n, two outcomes per trial, constant p, independent trials
Write P(X = x) = C(n, x) pˣ qⁿ⁻ˣ and name every symbol
Mean from Σ x P(x) using x C(n, x) = n C(n−1, x−1); answer np
Variance from E(X²) − (E(X))²; answer npq
Shape: symmetric at p = 0.5, right-skewed for small p, left-skewed for large p

bank.q: Define the Poisson distribution. Obtain it as a limiting case of the binomial distribution and give its mean and variance.
outline: Statement of the pmf P(X = x) = e^(−λ) λˣ ÷ x!
Set λ = np, let n → ∞ and p → 0 with λ fixed
Expand C(n, x) pˣ qⁿ⁻ˣ and apply the limits (1 − λ/n)ⁿ → e^(−λ)
Mean = variance = λ, so standard deviation is √λ
Two or three examples of rare-event counts: defects, accidents, calls

bank.q: Define the exponential distribution, derive its mean and variance, and prove the memoryless property.
outline: Density f(x) = λ e^(−λx), x ≥ 0, and CDF F(x) = 1 − e^(−λx)
Mean 1/λ by integration by parts, variance 1/λ²
Write the conditional probability in ratio form
Use P(X > s + t) = e^(−λ(s+t)) and P(X > s) = e^(−λs)
The ratio is e^(−λt) = P(X > t): the proof ends here

bank.q: List the properties of the normal distribution and explain how the standard normal table is used to find any normal probability.
outline: Density formula with μ and σ written out and symbols defined
Symmetry about x = μ, mean = median = mode, total area 1
Points of inflexion at μ ± σ; the curve never touches the axis
Any linear combination of independent normals is normal
z = (x − μ)/σ, then read the table; P(X ≤ a) = Φ((a − μ)/σ)
Use of the complementary rule and of P(a ≤ X ≤ b)

bank.q: Distinguish the geometric and negative binomial distributions, and state the mean and variance of each.
outline: Geometric = trials up to the first success; negative binomial = trials up to the r-th success
Write both pmfs and define the support
Geometric is the special case r = 1 of the negative binomial
Means 1/p and r/p; variances q/p² and rq/p²
Both are memoryless in the discrete sense

bank.q: A machine produces bolts of which 5% are defective. In a box of 20 bolts, find the probability that exactly 2 are defective and the probability that at most 2 are defective. State the mean and standard deviation of the defect count.
outline: Recognise a binomial with n = 20, p = 0.05, q = 0.95
Mean np = 1, variance npq = 0.95, standard deviation ≈ 0.975
Comment that the Poisson with λ = 1 gives a close check

bank.q: Telephone calls reach an office at an average rate of 3 per minute. Assuming a Poisson process, find the probability of exactly 5 calls in a minute, of no calls in a minute, and of at least 2 calls in two minutes.
outline: State X ~ Poisson(λ) with λ = 3 per minute
For two minutes take λ = 6 and compute 1 − P(0) − P(1) ≈ 0.9826
Note that the rate scales linearly with the length of the interval

bank.q: A student answers a multiple-choice test by guessing; each question has 4 options. Find the probability that the first correct answer is on the fifth question, and the expected number of questions until the first correct answer.
outline: Geometric model with p = 0.25, q = 0.75
Mean 1/p = 4 questions
Variance q/p² = 12, standard deviation ≈ 3.46
Interpret the mean as a long-run average over many attempts

bank.q: A city bus on a route arrives uniformly anywhere between 0 and 20 minutes after you reach the stop. Find the probability you wait between 5 and 12 minutes, the mean wait, and the standard deviation of the wait.
outline: Uniform U(0, 20); density 1/20
Probability = (12 − 5)/20 = 0.35
Mean (0 + 20)/2 = 10 minutes
Variance (20 − 0)²/12 = 33.33, standard deviation ≈ 5.77 minutes
Explain that probability here is an area of a rectangle

bank.q: The marks in a paper are normally distributed with mean 58 and standard deviation 12. Find the probability that a student scores above 75, and the mark exceeded by the top 10% of students.
outline: For the top 10%, find z with Φ(z) = 0.90, so z ≈ 1.2816
State the table values used and round sensibly

bank.q: Compare the binomial and Poisson distributions. Explain when the Poisson approximation is justified, and check it numerically for n = 100, p = 0.02 at x = 3.
outline: Binomial: fixed n, parameter p; Poisson: count over a continuum of trials, parameter λ
Binomial variance npq < np = mean; Poisson variance equals mean
Approximation is good when n ≥ 20 or so, p ≤ 0.05, np moderate
Poisson value with λ = 2: e^(−2) 2³ ÷ 3! ≈ 0.1804
Comment on the small difference and on when it becomes unsafe

bank.q: A component's lifetime is modelled by the exponential distribution. Discuss whether this is a reasonable model, and compare it with the Weibull and log-normal alternatives for wear-out and for multiplicative damage.
outline: Exponential has a constant hazard rate; suitable for random failures, not for ageing
Memoryless property and what it means physically
Weibull shape k: k < 1 infant mortality, k = 1 exponential, k > 1 wear-out
Log-normal arises from products of small positive effects; right-skewed, heavy tail
How to choose: plot failure data, check hazard shape, use goodness of fit
Recommendation with justification for each of the three regimes

bank.q: Explain the memoryless property in both the geometric and the exponential distributions. Show the discrete and continuous proofs and give one real situation where the property fails.
outline: Discrete statement P(X > m + n | X > m) = P(X > n) with q powers
Continuous statement with the exponential ratio of survival functions
Both hold because of the constant hazard rate
Example where it holds: calls in a Poisson process after a random time
Example where it fails: a machine that wears out, or a battery near end of life
Conclude that memorylessness is a modelling assumption, not a law of nature

bank.q: Explain the normal approximation to the binomial distribution with continuity correction. Apply it to n = 200, p = 0.4 to estimate P(X ≤ 70) and compare with the exact answer.
outline: Conditions: np ≥ 5 and nq ≥ 5, better when p is near 0.5
Mean np = 80, variance npq = 48, standard deviation ≈ 6.93
Use the continuity correction: P(X ≤ 70) becomes P(X ≤ 70.5)
Exact binomial ≈ 0.0846; state the size of the error
Why the correction matters when n is only moderately large

bank.q: Two identical components work independently, each with exponential lifetime of mean 1000 hours. Find the probability that a series system survives 500 hours and that a parallel system survives 500 hours. Comment on the design conclusion.
outline: λ = 1/1000 per hour; P(single survives 500 h) = e^(−0.5) ≈ 0.6065
Series: product of the two probabilities ≈ 0.3679
Show the general formulas p² and 1 − (1 − p)²
Comment: redundancy raises short-run survival sharply but costs double
Note the independence and constant-hazard assumptions and their limits

glossary.def: A rule that assigns a real number to each outcome of a random experiment.
A random variable whose possible values can be listed, such as a count.
A random variable whose values fill an interval, such as a time or a length.
The function P(X = x) giving the probability of each value of a discrete random variable.
A function f(x) whose area over an interval gives the probability that a continuous variable lies in that interval.
F(x) = P(X ≤ x), the probability of all values up to x.
A fixed number in a probability law, such as p, λ, μ or σ, that selects one member of the family.
Two events are independent when P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
The long-run average of a random variable, written E(X) or μ.
E(X²) − (E(X))², the average squared distance of the variable from its mean.
The positive square root of the variance, in the same units as the variable.
A measure of how lopsided a distribution is; a long right tail means positive skew.
A table of Φ(z) = P(Z ≤ z) for the N(0, 1) distribution, used after converting to z.
z = (x − μ)/σ, the number of standard deviations x lies from the mean.
A counting process in which events occur independently at a constant average rate.
The instantaneous failure rate at time t given survival up to t.
A parameter that stretches or shrinks the axis, such as b − a, 1/λ or λ in the Weibull.
A parameter that changes the form of the curve, such as α in the gamma or k in the Weibull.
Γ(α) = ∫₀^∞ xᵅ⁻¹ e^(−x) dx, with Γ(n) = (n − 1)! for a positive integer n.
Adding or subtracting 0.5 when a discrete count is approximated by a continuous curve.
S(t) = P(X > t), the probability that a lifetime or wait exceeds t.
The probability that a component or system performs its function for a stated time.
